mcqs.question: Why is an ARP request sent as a broadcast, while the ARP reply is sent as a unicast?
options: The requester doesn't yet know which specific host owns the target IP, so it must ask everyone; only the owning host needs to respond, so it can reply directly
Broadcasting is required by the Ethernet standard for all ARP traffic in both directions
Unicast replies are faster because they use a different physical transmission speed
It's arbitrary — either direction could use either delivery method with no functional difference
mcqs.explanation: The asymmetry is purely functional: the sender has no idea which host to address directly (hence broadcast to everyone), but once the owning host is identified, only it needs to answer, so a direct unicast reply suffices. There's no standard requiring symmetric delivery methods (option 2), no speed difference from unicast vs broadcast (option 3), and the choice is deliberate, not arbitrary (option 4).

mcqs.question: Why does ARP spoofing work at all — what design property of ARP does it exploit?
options: ARP encrypts replies with a weak, crackable cipher that attackers can break
ARP has no authentication mechanism, so any device can send a reply claiming ownership of any IP address, and receiving hosts trust it by default
ARP requires a password that attackers commonly guess
ARP only works over Wi-Fi, which is inherently insecure compared to wired connections
mcqs.explanation: The root exploit is the total absence of authentication — ARP replies are trusted purely because they arrived, with no way to verify the sender actually owns the claimed IP. ARP has no encryption to break (option 1), no password mechanism (option 3), and the vulnerability applies equally to wired and wireless LANs (option 4 is false).

mcqs.question: A colleague says "ARP and DNS are basically the same thing since they both resolve addresses." What's the key flaw in that statement?
options: Nothing — they are functionally identical protocols with different names
ARP resolves IP-to-MAC purely within one local LAN segment with no hierarchy; DNS resolves hostname-to-IP globally through a hierarchical, cached system spanning the whole internet
DNS is actually a layer-2 protocol just like ARP
ARP has a more complex hierarchy of root, TLD, and authoritative resolvers than DNS
mcqs.explanation: The scope and structure are fundamentally different: ARP is a flat, local-only protocol with no hierarchy, while DNS is global and hierarchical with caching across many layers of resolvers. They are not functionally identical (option 1 false), DNS operates at the application layer, not layer 2 (option 3 false), and it's DNS, not ARP, that has the root/TLD/authoritative hierarchy (option 4 reverses the facts).
